metadata.database: VEDA AyurMind AI — Disease-Herb Indication Database
metadata.source: Dravyaguna Vijñāna (Dravya_guna3_med_p2.pdf) — Appendix: Therapeutic (Disease-Wise) Indication of Drugs
metadata.notes: Botanical names sourced from classical Ayurvedic reference cross-matched with standard pharmacognosy. Sanskrit terms sourced from Pharmacological Glossary (P–Y section, same volume).

diseases.description: Reduced digestive fire causing impaired digestion, bloating, heaviness after meals, and accumulation of undigested food (āma). One of the root causes of most diseases in Ayurveda.

herbs.name: Caturbīja
herbs.botanical: Combination of four seeds (Ajamoda, Yavani, Shatapushpa, Sarsapa)

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Digestive — for food, āma, vikṛti; maturation; suppuration
Promoting desire for food and relish; appetite stimulant

diseases.description: A condition characterised by pallor, weakness, breathlessness, and reduced haemoglobin. In Ayurveda, linked to improper digestion, vitiation of rakta dhātu, and deficiency of rasa. Caused by poor nutrition, blood loss, or parasites.

herbs.name: Daśamūla
herbs.botanical: Group of ten roots (Bilva, Syonaka, Gambhari, Patala, Ganikarika, Salaparni, Prsniparni, Brhati, Kantakari, Goksura)

herbs.name: Laghupañcamūla
herbs.botanical: Group of five smaller roots (Salaparni, Prsniparni, Brhati, Kantakari, Goksura)

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Producing paleness in skin (restoring normal colour)

diseases.description: Loss of appetite and desire for food. In Ayurveda caused by agnimāndya, excess kapha or pitta, and mental stress. Characterised by aversion to all foods or specific foods.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Promoting desire for food and relish
Promoting desire for food and relish
Alleviating feeling of satiety (removes false fullness)

diseases.description: Loss of appetite specifically during pregnancy, causing nutritional deficiency for both mother and foetus. A sub-condition of obstetric disorders in Ayurveda.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Promoting desire for food and relish

diseases.description: Conditions involving reduced sexual vitality, low libido, premature ejaculation, oligospermia, and general reproductive weakness. Vājīkaraṇa is also one of the eight branches of Aṣṭāṅga Āyurveda.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Aphrodisiac; making one strong as a horse (vāji)

diseases.description: Inflammation of joints with pain, swelling, and restricted movement. General arthritis (not rheumatoid) caused by vāta vitiation and accumulation of āma in joint spaces.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Pacifying vāta heated in dhātus and skin

diseases.description: Difficulty in breathing, wheezing, and chest constriction. In Ayurveda, śvāsa has five types and is caused by vitiated vāta and kapha obstructing the respiratory channels (prāṇavaha srotas). Triggered by cold, dust, allergens, and ama.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Haemorrhoids with active bleeding, characterised by bright red blood with stool, pain during defecation, and general weakness due to blood loss. A sub-type of arśa (piles) involving rakta vitiation.
Painful pus-filled swellings on the skin caused by bacterial infection of hair follicles or oil glands. Ayurvedically linked to vitiation of rakta and kapha, poor digestion, and accumulation of āma.
Abnormal bony outgrowths (spurs, exostoses) developing on bones. In Ayurveda linked to vitiated asthi dhātu (bone tissue) and aggravated vāta.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Bony growth; enlargement of bone tissue

diseases.description: Skin damage from heat, fire, or hot substances. Classified in Ayurveda into four degrees. Management focuses on cooling, wound-healing, preventing infection, and skin regeneration.
Generalised burning sensation in the body, palms, soles, or urinary tract. A key symptom of pitta aggravation. May accompany fever, acid disorders, raktapitta, and urinary conditions.

Formation of stone-like concretions in the kidneys, ureters, bladder, or gallbladder. Caused by metabolic imbalance, concentrated urine, and improper diet. In Ayurveda linked to vitiated vāta, pitta, and kapha forming different types of stones.

herbs.name: Pañcatṛṇamūla
herbs.botanical: Group of five grass roots (Kusha, Kasha, Sara, Iksu, Darbha)

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating diseases of kidney and urinary bladder

diseases.description: Pain in the cardiac region — encompasses angina, pericarditis, and functional cardiac pain. In Ayurveda linked to vitiated vāta in the heart region (hṛdaya) and obstruction of prāṇavaha srotas.

Opacity of the crystalline lens leading to progressive loss of vision. In Ayurveda considered an advanced stage of timira (visual impairment) caused by vitiated pitta and kapha obstructing the lens (liṅga).
Pain in the chest region — includes pleuritis, costochondritis, musculoskeletal chest pain, and referred cardiac pain. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta and pitta in the urax (chest region).

Persistent low-grade or intermittent fever lasting more than two weeks. Causes weakness, emaciation, and depletion of body tissues. In Ayurveda a serious condition requiring rasāyana therapy after clearing the underlying doṣa.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Rejuvenative; promotive therapy for restoration after chronic illness

diseases.description: Severe cramping abdominal pain. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta obstructing the gut channels. Includes intestinal colic, renal colic, and biliary colic. Sub-types include ādhmāna (flatulent colic) and śūla in different anatomical locations.

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Immediately alleviating pain; fast acting analgesic

diseases.description: Acute severe pain in the right upper abdomen radiating to the back, caused by gallstones or bile duct spasm. A sub-type of śūla specifically involving the pitta organ system.

Secondary complications arising during or after fever — including dehydration, weakness, digestive disturbances, delirium, and residual ama. Management focuses on supporting recovery and removing lingering pathogenic factors.
Inflammation of the conjunctiva causing redness, discharge, itching, and swelling. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and kapha affecting the eye. Can be acute or chronic, infectious or allergic.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating diseases of eye caused by kapha

diseases.description: Infrequent, hard, or painful bowel movements. In Ayurveda primarily a vāta disorder causing dryness and obstruction in the pakvāśaya (large intestine). Leads to āma accumulation and secondary diseases.

Wasting disease characterised by chronic cough, haemoptysis, night sweats, fever, and emaciation. The Ayurvedic equivalent of tuberculosis. Called rājayakṣmā (the king of diseases) in classical texts due to its severity.

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

herbs.name: Parṇī catuṣṭaya
herbs.botanical: Group of four leafy herbs (Salaparni, Prsniparni, Masaparni, Mudgaparni)

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Causing consumption (herb to avoid in this condition)

diseases.description: Herbal measures used to temporarily prevent conception. These were part of the classical Ayurvedic gynaecological tradition as non-permanent birth control options. Use only under qualified supervision.

Opacity or white scar on the cornea (the clear front surface of the eye) causing visual blurring. Can result from infection, trauma, or inflammation. In Ayurveda related to kapha accumulation in the netrapaṭala.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating diseases of paṭals in eyes
Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Acute viral infection of the upper respiratory tract with runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, and mild throat irritation. In Ayurveda primarily a kapha-vāta disorder affecting the head channels (śiraḥ srotas).

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Herbal formulations and practices for enhancing skin tone, complexion, hair quality, and overall beauty. A recognised branch of Ayurveda closely related to svastha vṛtta (preventive health) and rasāyana therapy.

Persistent cough, which in Ayurveda may be vataja, pittaja, kaphaja, kṣataja, or kṣayaja types based on the underlying doṣa. One of the most commonly treated respiratory conditions, often accompanying colds, asthma, and bronchitis.

herbs.name: Mahatpañcamūla
herbs.botanical: Group of five larger roots (Bilva, Syonaka, Gambhari, Patala, Ganikarika)

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

diseases.description: Abnormal tissue growths, benign cysts, and tumours. Granthi refers to benign nodular growths; arbuda to more aggressive tumour-like formations. Both involve vitiated doṣas accumulating in specific tissues.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Breaking faecal mass or abdominal lump; Incision (surgical process)

diseases.description: Flaky, itchy scalp with excessive shedding of dead skin cells. In Ayurveda a vāta-pitta or vāta-kapha disorder of the scalp. Associated with dryness, poor oil secretion, and sometimes fungal involvement.
Loss of hearing — partial or complete. In Ayurveda primarily caused by vitiated vāta in the śrotraindriya (hearing sense organ), or by kapha obstruction. Can also result from chronic ear infections.

Progressive dimness of vision, colour distortion, and visual defects. Timira is the Ayurvedic umbrella term for visual disorders. At early stage (timira), intermediate stage (kāca), and advanced stage (liṅganāśa/cataract).
Tooth decay caused by bacterial acid erosion of tooth enamel. In Ayurveda attributed to kṛmi (worms/microbes) in the oral cavity, vitiated kapha, and excess sweet/sour foods.
Painful eruption of teeth in infants. The teething process in children associated with fever, irritability, drooling, and gum inflammation.
Infected boils, carbuncles, and skin ulcers occurring as a complication of diabetes (prameha). In Ayurveda, high blood sugar creates an environment conducive to kṛmi proliferation in skin tissues.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Anti-diabetic; alleviating prameha group of diseases

diseases.description: Frequent loose or watery stools. Ayurveda classifies six types: vātaja, pittaja, kaphaja, tridoṣaja, bhayaja, and śokaja. Causes include improper food, infections, stress, and season changes. Severe diarrhoea leads to dehydration and dhātu kṣaya (tissue depletion).

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Checking frequency and liquidity of stool; anti-diarrhoeal

diseases.description: Diarrhoea accompanied by blood in the stool — indicates involvement of rakta dhātu. Can result from dysentery, inflammatory bowel disease, or severe intestinal infection. Requires urgent management.

herbs.name: Nyagrodhādigaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group of five fig trees (Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Asvattha, Plaksha, Madhuka)

diseases.description: Obstructed or prolonged labour where the foetus fails to descend and deliver normally. Requires herbs that promote uterine contractions and ease delivery. Classical Ayurvedic obstetrics (prasūtitantra) gives detailed protocols.

General category for ear diseases including otitis media, otitis externa, tinnitus, discharge, and reduced hearing. In Ayurveda primarily vāta disorders of the śrotraindriya affecting the karṇa (ear).

herbs.name: Pañcavalkala
herbs.botanical: Group of five barks (Vata, Udumbara, Asvattha, Plaksha, Parisa)

diseases.description: General category encompassing all eye disorders — conjunctivitis, iritis, glaucoma, pterygium, dry eye, and infections. In Ayurveda the eye is governed by pitta (tejas) and alochaka pitta specifically. 80 types of eye diseases are described.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating diseases of paṭals in eyes
Alleviating diseases of eye caused by kapha

diseases.description: General oral diseases including stomatitis, mouth ulcers, gum inflammation, bad breath, and oral infections. Ayurveda identifies 66 types of mukharoga involving the lips, gums, tongue, teeth, palate, and throat.

herbs.name: Pañcapallava
herbs.botanical: Group of five tender leaves (Mango, Jackfruit, Jamun, Fig, Banyan)

diseases.description: General nasal diseases including sinusitis, nasal polyps, epistaxis, allergic rhinitis, and atrophic rhinitis. In Ayurveda, the nose is the gateway to the head and brain channels (śiraḥ srotas).

General dental disorders including tooth sensitivity, periodontal disease, gingivitis, loose teeth, and tooth pain. Ayurveda attributes dental problems to imbalanced vāta, kapha, and rakta affecting the mukhavaha srotas.

Throat diseases including pharyngitis, laryngitis, and sore throat. In Ayurveda linked to vitiated kapha, pitta, and vāta in the gala region. Hoarseness, pain, difficulty swallowing, and excessive mucus are cardinal symptoms.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Severe diarrhoea with mucus and blood, accompanied by intense intestinal cramps and tenesmus. In Ayurveda categorised as āmātisāra (with āma) caused by infection and accumulation of undigested matter in the gut.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Checking frequency and liquidity of stool; anti-diarrhoeal

diseases.description: Painful, burning, or difficult urination. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and vāta affecting the mūtravaha srotas. Can result from urinary tract infections, kidney stones, enlarged prostate, or chronic vāta imbalance.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating diseases of kidney and urinary bladder

diseases.description: Pain in the ear — may be sharp, throbbing, or aching. Caused by infections (otitis), referred pain from jaw or throat, or barometric pressure changes. In Ayurveda primarily a vāta disorder affecting the śrotraindriya.
Herbal measures to facilitate smooth, painless, and timely delivery. Given in the final trimester to prepare the birth canal, soften tissues, and regulate uterine contractions for a safe delivery.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating disorders of female genital organs

diseases.description: Chronic inflammatory skin condition with itching, redness, dryness, and vesicles. In Ayurveda classified as one of the kṣudra kusṭha (minor skin diseases), primarily caused by vitiated vāta and pitta with kapha involvement.

Extreme thinness and loss of body mass from disease, malnutrition, or excessive physical/mental activity. In Ayurveda caused by deficiency of all seven dhātus, especially rasa and māṁsa. Often a complication of chronic illness.
Swelling or elongation of the uvula causing throat discomfort, choking sensation, and difficulty swallowing or speaking. In Ayurveda a kapha-dominant condition of the gala region.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Recurrent seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Apasmāra in Ayurveda is described as a condition of periodic loss of consciousness with convulsions, caused by vitiated tridoṣa affecting the hṛdaya and manas (mind-heart axis). Four types are described.
Bleeding from the nose — spontaneous or trauma-induced. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta (rakta) ascending upward or trauma to the nāsā region. May also occur in raktapitta conditions.

A spreading superficial bacterial skin infection with distinct raised borders, redness, and systemic symptoms. In Ayurveda visarpa is classified into seven types based on dominant doṣa and involves spreading inflammation of the skin and subcutaneous tissue.

Abnormally high digestive fire causing constant hunger, rapid digestion, and emaciation despite eating. The Ayurvedic equivalent of conditions like hyperthyroidism and diabetes insipidus where tissues are consumed excessively.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Causing loss of digestive power (to moderate excessive agni)

diseases.description: Abnormal excessive tearing of the eyes. Can be caused by blocked tear ducts, irritation, entropion, or ectropion. In Ayurveda linked to kapha vitiation in the eye channels.
Abnormally excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) affecting quality of life. In Ayurveda caused by excess pitta, metabolic heat, and āma accumulation in svedavaha srotas (sweat channels).
Pain in or around the eye — may indicate glaucoma, optic neuritis, scleritis, or inflammation. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta and pitta in the eye.

Multiple eruptive boils, vesicular eruptions, and papular skin lesions. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated rakta and pitta causing skin eruptions. Includes chickenpox-like rashes, furuncles, and vesicular eruptions.

Temporary loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain. Ayurveda classifies mūrcchā into vātaja, pittaja, kaphaja, tridoṣaja, and madya (alcohol) types. Caused by fear, heat, anaemia, cardiac issues, or intoxicants.
